label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article I, Section 1. The lawmaking powers the Constitution grants are given to Congress, which is a Senate and a House. It reads: “All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”
This story is about whether imposing sanctions is an exercise of legislative power vested only in Congress.
The Constitution, signed on September 17, 1787, says "All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States."
The Constitution, signed on September 17, 1787, lets Congress make the laws needed to carry out powers vested in the Government of the United States "or in any Department or Officer thereof."

In 1794, the joint resolution of March 26, 1794 provided "that the President of the United States be authorized to give such instructions to the revenue officers of the United States, as shall appear best adapted for carrying the said resolution into full effect."

In 1789, section 2 of the Act of September 2, 1789, creating the Treasury Department, charged the Secretary of the Treasury "generally to perform all such services relative to the finances, as he shall be directed to perform."
Mohammadhossein Servati and Mojtaba Arabnejad were sanctioned for oil work.

The strongest argument against this is that vesting all legislative powers in Congress still allows laws that empower a department to perform directed services relative to the finances, so such departmental action does not itself exercise the legislative power.
We read this clause to mean Congress alone holds all lawmaking power the Constitution grants.
We read this clause to mean a department may announce sanctions only under authority a statute gives it.
This structure keeps the sovereign people in charge of the rules.
